references.title: Jet nose: curved wedges hung sideways on side-stud bricks, cone spike on an axle

discovery.description: Red and black forward fuselage section with sloped inverted bricks and curved white panels forming the nose cone.

notes.lesson: A jet nose that tapers in two directions: the top with 4×1 curved slopes and 1×1 cheese slopes, the sides with 6×4 triple-curved wedges hung sideways on 1×4 side-stud bricks and jumper plates, and a 3×3 cone plus a 2×2 cone on a 5-long axle as the spike.
notes.construction: 69 parts in 1 step. A core of 2×6 bricks, 2×4/2×2 plates and 2×2 plates with holes carries two 30414 1×4 side-stud bricks; two 43712 6×4 triple-curved wedges and two 48183 3×4 wings sit on those side studs and on 3794a jumper plates. Two 42023 inverted curved slopes close the underside, two 61678 curved slopes and eight 54200 cheese slopes shape the top, a 3039pce printed radar slope is the instrument panel at the rear, and a 6233 cone with a 3942c cone ride a 32073 axle through a 32064b Technic brick.
notes.interfaces: Stud directions: 69 parts, 51 up, the wedges facing ±Z, the cones facing −X. The rear plate layer and the Technic brick are the interfaces to the fuselage; the instrument slope faces the canopy.
notes.parent_context: `5892 - Airplane.ldr` places it at (−490, −32, 0) with the identity matrix: the nose points −X, ahead of the canopy and above the retracting nose gear.
notes.reuse_notes: Use the pattern for any pointed nose: build a studs-up core one stud narrower than the fuselage, hang the curved side panels on side studs, and let a cone pair on an axle make the tip. Change the wedge part to change the curvature.

guide.parent_supplies: The fuselage front it stacks on, the canopy behind the instrument slope and the nose-gear bay below.
guide.corrected_description: Accurate: a red and black nose with inverted curved slopes under it and curved white wedge panels on the sides. The spike is two cones on an axle.
guide.board_reading: Panel 1: a ghosted close-up of the fuselage front with the nose highlighted. Panel 2: the isolated nose from home, cheese slopes along the top edges and the radar slope at the rear. Panel 3: from the right, the cone tip face-on inside the wedge outline. Panel 4: the stud map, core up (lilac), wedges aqua (−Z), cones orange (−X).
guide.limits: Clutch of the wedges on the side studs and the cone pair's fit on the axle were not checked.

references.title: Retracting nose gear on liftarms, worked by a switch arm in the parent

discovery.description: Retractable nose landing gear using liftarms, axles, and a small rubber tyre on a grooved wheel rim.

notes.lesson: A nose leg that can swing: one bent 2×4 liftarm carries the wheel on a 2-long axle at its tip, two thin 4×0.5 liftarms and two 2×0.5 liftarms form a parallel link, and axle pins at the top are the pivot the parent holds.
notes.construction: 12 parts in 1 step: a 32140 bent liftarm, a 42610 rim with 51011 tyre on a 32062 axle at the bent end, two 32449 thin liftarms and two 41677 thin liftarms linked by two more 2-long axles, and two 43093 axle pins at the pivot end.
notes.interfaces: Stud directions: 12 parts, liftarms facing −Z and +X, wheel axle along X. The two axle pins and the free ends of the thin liftarms are the interfaces; the parent's switch arm pulls the link.
notes.parent_context: `5892 - Airplane.ldr` places it at (−390, −46, 0) with a matrix rotated about 175° about Z, so the leg hangs under the nose tilted 5° forward in the extended pose. The parent also holds `5892 - Switch arm.ldr` (two bent 32009 liftarms) that works the link to retract it.
notes.reuse_notes: Use it for any nose or tail wheel that must fold: keep the pivot pins on the frame, the parallel link to a lever, and check the wheel's swept path through the fuselage opening. Draw both poses before claiming retraction.

guide.parent_supplies: The pin holes for the pivot, the switch arm that moves the link, and the opening in the nose the wheel swings into.
guide.corrected_description: Accurate: a retractable nose leg on liftarms with one small wheel. Only the extended pose is drawn.
guide.board_reading: Panel 1: a ghosted close-up under the nose with the leg highlighted, hanging down and slightly forward. Panel 2: the isolated leg from home, bent liftarm, link and wheel. Panel 3: from the right, the wheel face-on between the blue axle pins. Panel 4: the stud map, liftarms aqua (−Z) and the bent liftarm blue/orange.
guide.limits: Retraction travel, the switch-arm linkage and the wheel's clearance through the nose were not checked; one pose only.

references.title: Swept one-stud fin from stepped 45° slopes

discovery.description: Red vertical tail fin with angled slope bricks, a curved white tip, and translucent red accent plates.

notes.lesson: A one-stud-thick swept fin: a brick stack whose leading edge steps back one 2×1 45° slope per course, a dark grey rudder strip of inverted 75° slopes at the trailing edge, a shallow 18° slope as the root fillet and a 4×1 curved slope as the tip cap, all on a 1×10 plate.
notes.construction: 26 parts in 1 step: a 4477 1×10 plate base, 1×3, 1×2 and 1×1 bricks stepping back each course, six 3040b 2×1 45° slopes on the leading edge, two 2449 inverted 75° 2×1×3 slopes and a 3665b inverted slope at the trailing edge, a 60477 4×1 18° slope at the root, a 61678 curved slope on top and trans-red 1×1 plates with a tile as the tail light.
notes.interfaces: Stud directions: 26 parts, all up. The 1×10 plate's underside is the only interface; it sits on the fuselage spine studs.
notes.parent_context: `5892 - Airplane.ldr` places it at (90, −134, 0) with the identity matrix, on the rear fuselage centreline above the engines.
notes.reuse_notes: Use it for any single fin: keep the stack one stud thick, step the leading edge with 45° slopes and the trailing edge with inverted 75° slopes, and change the courses to change the sweep. A two-stud fin needs 2×2 slopes instead.

guide.parent_supplies: The fuselage spine studs the base plate sits on; the fin is not braced sideways.
guide.corrected_description: Accurate: a red fin of angled slope bricks with a curved white tip and trans-red light plates.
guide.board_reading: Panel 1: a ghosted close-up of the rear fuselage with the fin highlighted. Panel 2: the isolated fin from home, stepped leading edge and grey trailing strip. Panel 3: from the right, the fin is one stud thick. Panel 4: the stud map, everything up (lilac).
guide.limits: Sideways strength of the one-stud stack was not checked.

references.title: Studs-up delta wing from overlapped corner-cut plates with a Technic-brick root

discovery.description: Large left wing assembly with white and black plates, wing cutout elements, and a red accent stripe.

notes.lesson: A studs-up delta wing from corner-cut plates (8×8, 6×6, 4×6 and 4×4 without corners) overlapped two deep, tiles along the trailing edge, red curved-top bricks as the leading-edge fairing, and two 1×2 Technic bricks with handle and clip plates at the root as the fuselage interface.
notes.construction: 55 parts in 1 step: two 8×8 and three 6×6 corner-cut plates, a 4×6 and a 4×4 corner-cut plate and a 6×12 plate overlapped into a swept trapezoid, two 4×4 wings with cutout at the tip, 1×4 and 1×6 tiles along the trailing edge, three 2×4 and two 2×1 curved-top bricks in red along the leading edge, two 3700 Technic bricks, two 60478 handle plates and two 61252 clip plates at the root, a grille tile vent and a 1×1 plate as the tip light.
notes.interfaces: All studs up. The root Technic bricks' pin holes, the handle plates and the clip plates meet the fuselage frame; the plates' studs carry the parent's upper skin.
notes.parent_context: `5892 - Airplane.ldr` places it at (−90, −40, −120) with the identity matrix; the right wing is a separate mirrored section at +Z.
notes.reuse_notes: Use it for any swept plate wing: overlap corner-cut plates so every seam is bridged by the layer above, tile the trailing edge, fair the leading edge with curved bricks and give the root a Technic-brick spar for pins.

guide.parent_supplies: The fuselage frame with pins and bars for the root bricks, handles and clips, and the skin above the root.
guide.corrected_description: Accurate: a large left wing of white and black plates with wing cut-out elements and a red stripe.
guide.board_reading: Panel 1: the ghosted jet with the left wing highlighted. Panel 2: the isolated wing from home, red leading-edge fairing and root bricks. Panel 3: from the right, the wing is two plates thick with the fairing bricks above. Panel 4: the stud map, everything up.
guide.limits: Root pin engagement and the clip plates' hold were not checked.

references.title: Radial engine face and two-blade propeller on one geared axle

discovery.description: Propeller and drive: a two-blade technic rotor on a geared axle with belt wheel, bush, bevel gears and four reddish-brown wedge wings

notes.lesson: A radial engine face and propeller on one 6-long axle: eight cylinders, each a clip plate holding a round tile and round plate, clip onto a 2×2 octagonal rod frame; bevel gears and a belt wheel on the axle let the parent's drive spin it; the propeller is a 2-blade Technic rotor with two 2×4 wedge plates per blade for the wooden-prop profile.
notes.construction: 55 parts in 6 steps plus one child. Step 1: the 3706 axle with a 1×3 plate and bush. Step 2: the 4185a belt wheel and a 4032a round plate. Step 3: the 30033 octagonal rod frame with a 32198 bevel gear. Step 4: eight `step69-4` cylinders (6019 clip, 98138 round tile, 6141 round plate) around the frame. Step 5: the second round plate and gear. Step 6: the 32124 rotor with four 41770 wedge plates on its studs.
notes.interfaces: Stud directions: 55 parts, rotor and blades facing +Z (along the axle), cylinders angled around it. The axle end and the belt wheel are the interfaces to the fuselage's drive; the rotor's studs carry the blade plates.
notes.parent_context: `10226 - main.ldr` places it at (−220, −36, 0) with matrix 0 0 −1 / 0 1 0 / 1 0 0, turned 90° about Y so the axle points −X out of the nose. The fuselage supplies the front bearing and the crank that drives the gears.
notes.reuse_notes: Use it for any radial-engined propeller plane: the clip-and-round-tile cylinder is one part trio repeated around an octagonal frame, and the rotor's four studs take wedge plates to shape blades. Keep the engine face one plate ahead of the cowling.

guide.parent_supplies: The nose bearing the axle passes through, the crank and gears behind the belt wheel, and the cowling around the cylinders.
guide.corrected_description: Accurate for the propeller and drive; it omits the eight radial cylinders (the `step69-4` child) that make up the engine face.
guide.board_reading: Panel 1: a ghosted close-up of the nose with the propeller and cylinders highlighted. Panel 2: source step 2, the belt wheel on the axle. Panel 3: source step 4, the eight cylinder children around the octagonal frame. Panel 4: the stud map, blades blue (+Z), cylinders violet (angled), hub plates orange.
guide.limits: Gear meshing with the fuselage drive and the blade plates' clutch on the rotor studs were not checked.

references.title: Biplane landing gear: suspension-arm V struts and shock absorbers on an open beam frame, pulley-and-dish wheels

discovery.description: Technic beam framework: a 7x5 open-center beam joined by pins with two light-bluish-grey 1x6 tiles

notes.lesson: Biplane landing gear from Technic parts: a 7×5 open-centre beam frame pinned under the fuselage, two V struts of 1×9 suspension arms, two 6.5L shock absorbers as the sprung legs, and a 12-long axle through the V apexes carrying two 5D pulley wheels capped with 4×4 inverted dishes as the wheels.
notes.construction: 38 parts in 7 root steps and three children. Steps 1–2: the 64179 7×5 open-centre beam with half pins and 3/4 pins. Steps 3–4: two `step58-3` children (a 32294 suspension arm on a long pin) and the `shock` child (4254 rod in a 4255 cylinder) as the legs. Step 5: the `step58-5` child, a 3708 axle with two 3736 pulley wheels and two 3960 inverted dishes as wheels. Steps 6–7: the second V and two 1×6 tiles closing the frame.
notes.interfaces: Stud directions: frame tiles up, arms and wheels angled or along the axle. The beam frame's pin holes are the interface to the fuselage underside; the shock cylinders pin to the frame and the arms to the axle.
notes.parent_context: `10226 - main.ldr` places it at (−120, 12, 0) with matrix −1 0 0 / 0 −1 0 / 0 0 1, a 180° turn about Z: the frame goes against the fuselage belly and the wheels hang below, just behind the engine.
notes.reuse_notes: Rebuild the technique rather than copying: a pinned beam frame as the gear mount, suspension arms as struts, shocks as legs, and pulley-plus-dish wheels for a vintage look. The shock's spring is drawn as raw mesh geometry in the source, which is why this is an inspiration entry.

guide.parent_supplies: The fuselage belly with the pin holes the frame hangs from, and the engine cowling ahead of it.
guide.corrected_description: Partly accurate: the 7×5 open-centre beam and two tiles are there, but the section is the complete landing gear with V struts, shock absorbers, axle and dish wheels.
guide.board_reading: Panel 1: a ghosted close-up under the fuselage with the gear highlighted below the lower wing. Panel 2: source step 2, the open beam frame with its pins. Panel 3: source step 5, the axle child with pulley wheels and dishes between the V struts. Panel 4: the stud map, the frame lilac, arms and wheels angled.
guide.limits: Inspiration only: the shock child's spring is raw mesh geometry (coverage.raw_geometry, geometry.nonplanar), so source checks fail and export is blocked. Suspension travel and wheel rotation were not checked.

references.title: Biplane upper wing: plate spar, 1×3 tile planking, socket plates for the ailerons and suspension-arm struts

discovery.description: Large dark-green plank-and-tile main wing on a tan plate base with socket joints, towball pins and wedge wings

notes.lesson: The upper wing of the biplane: a sandwich of 2×16 plates and 6×10 plates as the spar, rows of dark-green 1×3 tiles with gaps as the planked fabric-and-rib surface, 6×6 tiles as the aileron bays, two socket plates per side that take the ailerons' towballs, and four 1×9 suspension arms pinned underneath as the interplane struts.
notes.construction: 136 parts in 12 root steps and six children. Steps 1–7: alternating 2×16, 2×8 and 6×10 plate layers with 2×2 plates with holes and Technic tiles with holes at the strut stations. Step 8: two 10202 6×6 tiles as the aileron bays. Steps 9–11: thirty-two 1×3 tiles in rows as the planking and the `step53-11` children (a 63082 socket plate pair) for the aileron balls. Step 12: four `step53-13` children (a 32294 suspension arm on a 2×2 plate with holes) as the struts, plus the `string8` and `string9` rigging children from string-end studs.
notes.interfaces: All studs up except the angled struts. The struts' lower pin holes meet the lower wing and the cabane; the socket plates take the aileron towballs; the string-end studs anchor the rigging.
notes.parent_context: `10226 - main.ldr` places it at (−170, −212, 0) with matrix −1 0 0 / 0 1 0 / 0 0 −1, a 180° turn about Y, above the fuselage; the lower wing, cabane struts and ailerons are separate sections.
notes.reuse_notes: Rebuild the technique: tile rows with one-stud gaps read as ribbed fabric on any vintage wing, socket plates give snap-in control surfaces, and suspension arms make slim interplane struts. The rigging strings are LDCad segments; add them last with the flex workflow.

guide.parent_supplies: The lower wing and cabane the struts land on, the ailerons that snap into the sockets, and the rigging anchors on the fuselage.
guide.corrected_description: Accurate: a dark-green plank-and-tile main wing on a tan plate base with socket joints, towball pins and wedge wings.
guide.board_reading: Panel 1: the ghosted biplane with the upper wing highlighted and its struts reaching down. Panel 2: source step 4, the plate layers with the first tan 6×10 plates. Panel 3: source step 8, the two 6×6 aileron-bay tiles. Panel 4: the stud map, everything up with the struts angled (rose).
guide.limits: Inspiration only: the two rigging-string children are LDCad segments with mirrored matrices (assembly.nonrigid, assembly.library_internal), so source checks fail and export is blocked. Strut engagement and socket clutch were not checked.

references.title: Tapered tailplane from a plate core and 3×12 wing plates, turned by the parent

discovery.description: Tailplane/horizontal stabilizer: large 3x12 left and right wings over slopes on a dark-bluish-grey plate base

notes.lesson: A tapered tailplane from a 6×12 plate core, two 3×12 wing plates as the swept halves, four 1×8 curved slopes as rounded tips and 33°/45° slopes at the leading edge; built with its span along X and turned 90° by the parent.
notes.construction: 25 parts in 6 steps. Steps 1–2: the 6×12 plate with brown 3298 33° and 3039 45° slopes along the leading edge and a 2×2 brick with 2×4 plates as the centre spar. Step 3: a 3709b 2×4 Technic plate and 2×6 plate at the rear. Step 4: the 47397/47398 3×12 wing plates as the tapered halves. Steps 5–6: four 85970 1×8 curved slopes along the tips and four 85984 cheese slopes on the leading edge.

notes.reuse_notes: Use it for any tapered stabiliser: a plate core, 3×12 wing plates for the taper, curved slopes for the tips. Build it in its own frame and let the parent place it; add the elevator with towball plates like the aileron package.

guide.parent_supplies: The rear fuselage it sits on and the rigging that meets the Technic plate's holes.

references.title: Aileron strip hinged on two towball plates

notes.lesson: An aileron as a two-plate-thick strip with a rounded tip: two 1×4 towball plates along its leading edge snap into the wing's ball sockets and form the hinge; a down bracket and tiles finish the root.

references.title: Biplane fuselage side wall: one-stud brick wall on a plate strip with hinge plates and a reinforced panel

discovery.description: Dark-tan brick-and-plate fuselage/cowling panel with hinge plates, a reinforced side panel and white clip bricks

notes.lesson: A biplane fuselage side as a one-stud-thick wall: dark-tan 1×4 and 1×1 bricks on a 1×8 plate strip, two 1×4 hinge-plate pairs so the wall folds to the fuselage taper, a reinforced 1×4×3 panel as the cockpit side, and a 1×1×3 clip brick that anchors a rigging string.

Steps 8–10: the 2429/2430 hinge plates at each end, plates on top and the 60583b clip brick with a string-end stud; the `string5` child is the rigging string.

notes.parent_context: `10226 - main.ldr` places it at (60, −16, 60) with matrix −1 0 0 / 0 1 0 / 0 0 −1, a 180° turn about Y, as the right-hand fuselage side beside the cockpit; `step35` is the mirrored left side.

references.title: Jet nacelle: fan, housing and cone on a thin plate pylon

discovery.description: A jet engine pod featuring a fan, engine housing, cone intake, and curved slope fairing.

notes.lesson: A convincing jet nacelle from three dedicated parts (43121 engine shell, 46667 fan on its own pin, 3942c cone as the exhaust) hung under the wing on a thin pylon: a 2×8 plate with a 6×2 curved slope and an inverted 33° slope as its fairing.
notes.construction: 12 parts in 2 steps. Step 1: the engine core, a 43121 shell with the 46667 fan pushed into its front, four bushes on the fan pin, and at the back a 2×2 round plate, a four-prong spider (LDraw part 2566, catalogued as an obsolete palm-tree top) and the 3942c cone pointing aft as the exhaust. Step 2: the pylon, a 2×8 plate laid along the engine with a 6×2 curved slope and an inverted 3×2 slope on top closing the fairing.
notes.interfaces: Stud directions: 12 parts, 10 up, 2 facing +Z (the round plate and cone on the exhaust axis). The pylon plate's studs are the only mounting interface; it meets the anti-studs under the 54093 wing. The fan turns on its pin; nothing else moves.
notes.parent_context: `7893 - plane.ldr` places it four times with the identity matrix at X ±220 (Z −80) and X ±380 (Z 0), all at Y 32: two engines per wing, the outboard pair one stud further aft. The wing underside supplies the anti-studs; the engines hang below the wing plane.
notes.reuse_notes: Use it for any twin- or four-engine airliner: keep the fan, shell and cone on one axis, mount through the pylon plate only, and space repeated engines along the wing sweep. Swap the pylon fairing slopes to change the pylon profile.

guide.parent_supplies: The 54093 wing with its underside anti-studs, and the sweep that staggers the outboard engine aft.
guide.corrected_description: A jet nacelle with the fan at the front and the cone as the exhaust at the back, not an intake; the four-prong black part at the rear is LDraw 2566, an obsolete palm-tree-top identity used as an exhaust spider.
guide.board_reading: Panel 1: the ghosted airliner with all four nacelles highlighted under the wings. Panel 2: the isolated nacelle from home, fan forward. Panel 3: from the right, the pylon plate and fairing on top, cone aft. Panel 4: the stud map, pylon and plates up (lilac), round plate and cone facing +Z (blue).
guide.limits: Fan rotation, pylon strength and the exhaust ring's attachment were not checked; part 2566 is an obsolete LDraw identity.

references.title: Four-wheel bogie on wheel-pin plates, mounted by one pin through standing tiles

discovery.description: A landing gear assembly of four wheels with tyres, wheel pins, and mounting plates.

notes.lesson: A compact main-gear bogie: two 2×2 wheel-pin plates under a 2×4 plate carry four small wheels; two 1×2 tiles with holes stand on the plate so that one friction pin through them is the whole mounting interface to the fuselage.
notes.construction: 14 parts in 1 step: a 2×4 plate on two 4870 2×2 plates with wheel pins, four 4624 rims with 3139 tyres pressed onto the pins, two 32530 1×2 tiles with two holes standing side by side on the plate, and a 2780 friction pin through their lower holes.
notes.interfaces: Stud directions: 14 parts, 7 up, the standing tiles and wheels facing ±Z. The pin is the only connection to the parent; the wheels turn on their pins.
notes.parent_context: `7893 - plane.ldr` places it twice with the identity matrix at Y 127, Z 64, X −150 and X +170: the two bogies are not symmetric about X=0 because the fuselage sections are offset one stud in the source. They hang under the wing root behind the engines.
notes.reuse_notes: Use it under any minifigure-scale airliner or cargo plane: one pin hole per bogie in the fuselage or wing is enough, and the standing tiles set the leg height. Mirror the placement, not the part.

guide.parent_supplies: A pin hole under each wing root at the right height; the bogie cannot stand on its own without it.
guide.corrected_description: Accurate: four wheels on two wheel-pin plates with a pin mount. The source places the two bogies 20 LDU off-centre from each other.
guide.board_reading: Panel 1: the ghosted airliner with both bogies highlighted under the wing roots. Panel 2: the isolated bogie from home, standing tiles on top. Panel 3: from the right, the four wheels, the plate and the two standing tiles with their holes. Panel 4: the stud map, plates up (lilac), tiles and wheels facing ±Z (blue and aqua).

references.title: Two-seat flight deck with instrument slopes

discovery.description: The cockpit interior with two pilot seats, flight control slopes, a radar display, instrument monitor, and console detailing.

notes.lesson: A two-seat flight deck that drops into a moulded nose: two 2×2 seats, two printed instrument slopes, bar control columns, grille tiles on side-stud bricks as side consoles and a 1×4 arch over the centre.
notes.construction: 22 parts in 2 steps. Step 1: a 6×10 plate with a 3×6 cut-corner plate ahead of it, 1×2 bricks as seat bases and two 48729a bar clips as control columns. Step 2: two 4079 seats, two 3039pc9 instrument slopes, two 52107 side-stud bricks with 2412b grille tiles as the side consoles, a 3659 1×4 arch on 1×2×2 bricks between the seats, a handle brick and a printed tile.
notes.interfaces: Stud directions: 22 parts, 16 up, the grille tiles facing −Z and the control columns angled. The base plates' underside is the interface; everything above is contained by the parent's nose section.
notes.parent_context: `7893 - plane.ldr` places it at (0, 8, −460) with the identity matrix, inside the 54092 moulded nose under its glazing.
notes.reuse_notes: Use it for any minifigure flight deck: seats, instruments and consoles on one plate, checked against the glazing height before closing the nose. Minifigure fit was not drawn; add pilots and check knees and headroom.

guide.parent_supplies: The moulded nose section with its glazing, floor sockets and the opening behind the deck.
guide.corrected_description: Accurate: two pilot seats, instrument slopes, a radar display tile and console detailing.
guide.board_reading: Panel 1: a ghosted close-up of the nose with the flight deck highlighted. Panel 2: the isolated deck from home. Panel 3: from the right, seats, columns, instrument slope and consoles in profile. Panel 4: the stud map, plates up (lilac), grille tiles aqua (−Z), columns violet (angled).
guide.limits: Minifigure seating, headroom under the glazing and the column's clip were not checked.

references.title: Openable cabin roof: hinged double-slope bricks on a window wall

discovery.description: Airplane subassembly featuring cockpit windows, transparent glass panes, and hinged slope sections.

notes.lesson: The openable roof of the classic City airliner: four 4×4 double-slope bricks with a hinge edge sit on one wall of window bricks; the opposite wall in the parent carries the matching hinge, so the whole roof lifts to load minifigures.
notes.construction: 16 parts in 3 steps. Step 1: a 12-stud wall of three 4863 1×4×2 windows with six 4862 glass panes. Step 2: a 1×8 and a 1×6 plate (and a 1×1 plate) capping the wall. Step 3: four 4857 4×4 double-slope hinge bricks forming the roof.
notes.interfaces: Stud directions: 16 parts, all up. The window wall's underside meets the fuselage floor plates; the hinge fingers on the far edge of the roof bricks meet the hinge on the parent's other wall.
notes.parent_context: `6392 - airplane.ldr` places it at (200, −156, −35) with matrix −1 0 0 / 0 1 0 / 0 0 −1, a 180° turn about Y: the section becomes the right-hand cabin wall and roof. The same design appears in 10159.
notes.reuse_notes: Use it when a cabin must open without removing the roof: one wall carries the roof bricks, the other the hinge, and the cabin width is fixed by the 4×4 double slopes (four studs across). Window bricks give the row of cabin windows for free.

guide.parent_supplies: The left-hand wall with the hinge counterpart, the floor plates and the end walls.
guide.corrected_description: Accurate: cabin windows with glass panes and hinged double-slope roof sections; they are cabin windows, not cockpit windows.
guide.board_reading: Panel 1: the ghosted classic airliner with the wall and roof highlighted along the cabin. Panel 2: source step 1, the window wall. Panel 3: source step 2, the capping plates. Panel 4: the stud map, everything up (lilac).
guide.limits: Hinge mating and the roof's opening clearance were not checked.

references.title: Two-cylinder piston engine under a liftarm cowling

discovery.description: Engine motor subassembly built from bent liftarms, cross blocks, bevel gears and a toggle-joint connector to transfer rotation.

notes.lesson: A two-cylinder engine for a Technic propeller plane: two pistons on connecting rods and a crank between cross blocks, driven through a bevel-gear pair from the propeller axle, in a white bent-liftarm cradle with eight axle joiners as exhaust stubs and a red beam-and-panel cowling on top.
notes.construction: 123 parts in 9 root steps and four children. Steps 1–3: a white 4×6 bent-liftarm cradle with axles, cross blocks and eight smooth axle joiners standing as exhaust stubs. Step 4: the `motor2` child, the two-cylinder block: red beams and black tooth plates as rocker covers over two 2851 pistons on 2852 rods and two 2853 crank pieces with a 12-tooth bevel gear. Steps 5–9: the `motorgears` child (a bevel pair on the long axle that runs to the propeller), the `motortop` cover of black beams and a white bent liftarm, and the `motorhood` red panels pinned over the cylinders.
notes.interfaces: Studless: friction pins, axle pins and cross blocks in every direction. The long axle out of the front of the gear child is the propeller shaft; the cradle's pin holes meet the nose frame.
notes.parent_context: `42040 - Fire Plane.ldr` places it at (−120, −175, −133) with a 90° turn about Y and a 3° roll, so the propeller axle points −Z out of the nose; the parent adds the three-blade 99012 rotor, the nose frame and the landing gear beneath.
notes.reuse_notes: Use it for a visible piston engine in any Technic prop plane: build cradle, crank and pistons first, then the covers and hood; mesh the bevel pair with the propeller axle and check piston travel before closing the cowling.

guide.parent_supplies: The propeller axle and rotor, the nose frame the cradle pins into, and the geared drive that turns the crank from the propeller.
guide.corrected_description: Partly accurate: bent liftarms, cross blocks, bevel gears and a toggle joint are there, but the section is the two-cylinder engine itself, with pistons, rods, crank and a red cowling.
guide.board_reading: Panel 1: the ghosted nose with the engine highlighted behind the propeller. Panel 2: source step 3, the white cradle with the grey axle joiners as exhaust stubs. Panel 3: source step 6, the red beams, pistons and bevel gear with the hood pins highlighted. Panel 4: the stud map, pins and liftarms in every direction.
guide.limits: Piston travel, the bevel mesh with the propeller axle and hood clearance were not checked.

references.title: Technic rear airframe: three spar beams carry the wings, fin and a joystick-geared stabiliser

discovery.description: Tail boom assembly with white trapezium panels, beams, a trans-red light tile and mounting cross blocks.

notes.lesson: How a studless plane hangs everything behind the cockpit off three parallel 9-long spar beams: a tall liftarm fin, a tilting stabiliser driven by knob gears from a cockpit joystick, trapezium-panel wings pinned to the spars, and panel tail sides.
notes.construction: 168 parts in 20 root steps and seven children. Steps 1–3: the fin, white liftarms pinned into a tall tapered frame. Step 4: the first red 9-long spar beam. Steps 5–12: the `hstab` child (a white panel on a short axle so it can tilt), the `tailgearing` child (five 4-knob gears on cross axles turning the stabiliser axle), more spar beams and axle joiners. Steps 13–20: the `wing1` and `wing2` children (a 5×11 trapezium panel on a beam with pins), the `joystick` child (a red lever on a gear hub with a towball), and the `tailside` panel children closing the rear fuselage.
notes.interfaces: Studless: 37 friction pins, axles and joiners. The three red spar beams and the pins on the tail sides connect to the front frame; the joystick turns knob gears that pitch the stabiliser axle; the wings pin onto the spar beams, not onto panels.
notes.parent_context: `42040 - Fire Plane.ldr` places it at (−140, −266, 413) with the identity rotation pitched 3° about X: it is the rear two-thirds of the airframe above the floor, seats, engine and landing gear that the parent supplies.
notes.reuse_notes: Use it to learn two things: keep the spar beams continuous and hang wings and tail off them, and route a cockpit lever to a tail surface through knob gears on cross axles. Check the stabiliser's travel before closing the tail sides.

guide.parent_supplies: The floor, seats, engine cradle, landing gear and the front frame the spar beams pin into.
guide.corrected_description: Partly accurate: it is a tail boom with trapezium panels and beams, but the section also carries both wings, the horizontal stabiliser, its knob-gear control train and the cockpit joystick.
guide.board_reading: Panel 1: the ghosted plane with the whole rear airframe highlighted: fin, stabiliser, spar beams and both wings. Panel 2: source step 7, the white stabiliser child on its axle beside the fin and the first red spar. Panel 3: source step 13, the right wing child highlighted on the spar beams with the gearing below. Panel 4: the stud map, beams and panels in every direction.
guide.limits: The joystick-to-stabiliser travel and the pin retention of the wings were not checked; one static pose.

references.title: Studded Technic wing: Technic-brick spars, wing-brick ribs, universal-joint roots and plate flaps

discovery.description: The main wings constructed from wing-front and wing-back Technic bricks, long plates, gears, and translucent indicator lights.

notes.lesson: A studded Technic wing: two 1×16 Technic bricks as leading and trailing spars on 10-long axles, 1×4 wing-front and 1×6 wing-back bricks as ribs, 1×8 plates as skin strips; each root is a universal joint with a towball so the wing can be tilted, and the flaps are 4×10 plates on a Technic-plate hinge with toggle joints.
notes.construction: 136 parts in 6 root steps and three children. Step 1: two 1×16 Technic bricks and four 10-long axles as the twin spar. Steps 2–3: ten 2743 wing-front bricks on the leading spar and ten 2744 wing-back bricks on the trailing spar as ribs. Step 4: 1×8 plates as skin strips and the `Wing joint left` and `right` children (a 3712 universal joint with its 3326a centre on the axle, a 2736 towball and 1×2 hole bricks). Steps 5–6: 8-tooth gears, half bushes and the two `Flap` children (a 4×10 plate on a 1×8 Technic plate with toggle joints) on the trailing edge.
notes.interfaces: Stud directions: ribs and plates up, the flaps angled. The universal joints on the spar axles and the towballs are the interfaces to the fuselage; the 8-tooth gears at the root take the parent's adjustment drive.
notes.parent_context: `8855 - Prop Plane.ldr` places it at (0, −365, 10) with the identity matrix: a high wing above the fuselage, with the pontoons below and the engine ahead.
notes.reuse_notes: Use the spar-and-rib pattern for any studded Technic wing: Technic-brick spars give the span and pin holes, wing bricks give the profile, plates the skin. Drop the universal joints unless the wing must tilt, and hinge flaps on a Technic plate.

guide.parent_supplies: The cabane bricks and towball sockets the wing sits on, and the control gears that meet the 8-tooth gears at the root.
guide.corrected_description: Partly accurate: wing bricks, long plates, gears and indicator lights are there; it omits the universal joints and towballs that make the wing adjustable and the two flap children.
guide.board_reading: Panel 1: the ghosted floatplane with the wing highlighted above the fuselage. Panel 2: source step 2, the wing-front bricks going onto the leading spar. Panel 3: source step 4, the 1×8 skin plates and the wing-joint children at the root. Panel 4: the stud map, ribs and plates up, the flaps angled (violet).
guide.limits: Wing tilt travel, flap travel and the universal joints' retention were not checked.

references.title: Twin floats on an axle-and-steering-arm truss, with wheels inside the floats

discovery.description: A pair of pontoon floats with sloped plating, axles, and rubber tyres mounted on yellow wheel rims.

notes.lesson: Twin floats for a studded Technic floatplane: each float is a pair of 1×16 Technic bricks with stepped 2×3 plates and an inverted-slope bow, carrying a wheel inside so the plane also rolls; the floats hang on a truss of 3-long axles joined by steering arms and toggle joints that set the strut angles.
notes.construction: 153 parts in 8 root steps and three children. Steps 1–2: two floats, each two 1×16 Technic bricks with 1×8 Technic plates, stepped 2×3 and 1×3 plates and 4287a inverted slopes at the bow. Step 3: 4261 steering arms and 3651 pin connectors standing on the floats. Steps 4–8: the `Pontoon joint 1`, `2` and `3` children (a steering arm, toggle joint and axle each) and 3-long axles with half bushes forming the A-frame truss, with the 3482 rims and 3483 tyres inside the floats on 6-long axles.
notes.interfaces: Studs up on the floats; the truss angled. The truss apex connectors meet the fuselage underside; the wheels turn on their axles inside the floats.
notes.parent_context: `8855 - Prop Plane.ldr` places it at (0, −0.35, 0) with the identity matrix: the floats are the lowest element, under the fuselage and ahead of the tail.
notes.reuse_notes: Rebuild the technique: Technic-brick floats give a long slim hull with pin holes for the truss; steering arms and toggle joints let axle struts meet at non-grid angles. One joint child keeps a skewed part from the original strained model, so this is inspiration only.

guide.parent_supplies: The fuselage underside the truss apexes pin into, and the wing above.
guide.corrected_description: Accurate: a pair of pontoon floats with sloped plating, axles and rubber tyres on yellow rims.
guide.board_reading: Panel 1: the ghosted floatplane with the floats and truss highlighted below the fuselage. Panel 2: source step 3, the steering arms and pin connectors standing on the two floats. Panel 3: source step 5, the joint children and axles forming the truss. Panel 4: the stud map, floats up, truss angled.
guide.limits: Inspiration only: `Pontoon joint 1` keeps two skewed placements from the author's strained physical model (assembly.nonrigid), so source checks fail and export is blocked. Truss geometry and wheel rotation were not checked.

references.title: Boxy studded Technic engine block with hole-brick crank bearings

discovery.description: A light grey and red Technic engine block built from bricks, plates, and slope pieces forming the cylindrical engine housing.

notes.lesson: A boxy studded Technic engine block: an H of plates, two 1×8 Technic bricks whose holes carry the propeller axle, red plates and bricks as the crankcase, and 1×3 bricks standing as cylinder banks with 45° slopes as the cowl.
notes.construction: 34 parts in 5 steps. Step 1: two 2×4 plates with two 2×2 corner plates in an H. Step 2: two 1×8 Technic bricks along the sides with two 1×2 hole bricks and two pins. Step 3: red 1×6, 1×4 and corner plates. Step 4: red 2×4 and 1×3 bricks as the crankcase. Step 5: grey 1×3 bricks standing as cylinder banks, two red 45° slopes and a 2×2 brick.
notes.interfaces: All studs up. The Technic-brick holes carry the parent's propeller axle and gears; the plate base stacks on the nose frame.
notes.parent_context: `8855 - Prop Plane.ldr` places it at (0, −229, −250) with the identity matrix, in the nose behind the propeller; the `Piston` and `Piston gear` children that move belong to the parent.
notes.reuse_notes: Use it as a quick studded engine block for a 1980s-style Technic plane: hole bricks on both sides give the crank bearing, and the block stays one stud narrower than the cowling.

guide.parent_supplies: The propeller axle, the piston and piston-gear sections and the cowling around the block.
guide.corrected_description: Partly accurate: a light grey and red engine block of bricks, plates and slopes, but boxy rather than cylindrical; the pistons and gears are separate sections.
guide.board_reading: Panel 1: the ghosted nose with the block highlighted behind the propeller. Panel 2: source step 2, the two 1×8 Technic bricks and pins on the plate H. Panel 3: source step 3, the red plate layer. Panel 4: the stud map, everything up.
guide.limits: Bearing alignment with the parent's axle was not checked.

references.title: Studded Technic empennage: 7×12 wing plates, jumper-plate fin and a control axle along the boom

discovery.description: An aircraft tail unit with left and right wing elements, sloped bricks, axles, and pin connectors forming the empennage.

notes.lesson: A studded Technic empennage: 7×12 wing plates as the tailplane halves on a short Technic-brick block, a one-stud fin of 45° slopes and jumper plates with a red stripe, and a `Tail body` boom of 1×12 and 1×6 Technic bricks; a long axle with toggle joints runs forward along the boom as the elevator control.
notes.construction: 71 parts in 5 root steps and one child. Step 1: two jumper plates. Step 2: the 3585/3586 7×12 wing plates on 1×4 hole bricks as the tailplane. Step 3: a long axle through the block with two toggle joints and half bushes, running forward. Step 4: the `Tail body` child, a boom of two 1×12, two 1×6 and four 1×4 Technic bricks with plates and pins. Step 5: the fin, 45° and inverted 45° slopes stepping up a 1×3 brick stack with jumper plates, a red plate stripe and a round brick at the top.
notes.interfaces: Studs up; the control axle angled. The boom's Technic bricks pin to the rear fuselage; the axle's toggle joint meets the parent's control run.
notes.parent_context: `8855 - Prop Plane.ldr` places it at (0, −304, 233) with the identity matrix pitched 0.4°: behind the wing and above the pontoons, with the boom entering the rear fuselage.
notes.reuse_notes: Use the 7×12 wing plates as one-part tailplane halves and the jumper-plate stack for a thin swept fin; run control axles along the boom inside the Technic bricks.

guide.parent_supplies: The rear fuselage the boom pins into and the control lever that drives the axle.
guide.corrected_description: Accurate: a tail unit with left and right wing elements, slope bricks, axles and pin connectors.
guide.board_reading: Panel 1: the ghosted floatplane with the tail highlighted at the rear. Panel 2: source step 2, the two 7×12 wing plates on the block. Panel 3: source step 3, the long control axle with its toggle joint running forward. Panel 4: the stud map, everything up with the axle angled.
guide.limits: Elevator travel and the axle's bearings in the boom were not checked.

references.title: Rolling boarding stairs

discovery.description: A yellow and black staircase assembly with handrail, four rolling wheels, and landing plates for passenger boarding.

notes.lesson: Rolling boarding stairs for a minifigure airliner: a dedicated 7×4×6 open staircase part on a 4×6 plate with wheel-pin plates and four small wheels, a 4×4 landing plate with two 1×4 panels as rails and an antenna as the handrail post.
notes.construction: 21 parts in 3 steps. Step 1: a 4×6 plate on two 1×4 wheel-pin plates, two 3×1 33° slopes and a 4H antenna. Step 2: the 30134 staircase with a locking hinge arm and plate and a jumper plate. Step 3: four 6.4×8 rims with tyres, a 4×4 landing plate and two 1×4×1 panels as rails.
notes.interfaces: Studs up; the staircase is one moulded part. Free-standing: nothing connects it to the aircraft, the parent only positions it at the door.
notes.parent_context: `7893 - main.ldr` places it at (168, −32, −332) turned 90° about Y, beside the open forward door of the airliner.
notes.reuse_notes: Use it as ground equipment beside any minifigure airliner door; set the landing height to the door sill before choosing the base plates.

guide.parent_supplies: Only the position beside the door; the stairs stand on their own wheels.
guide.corrected_description: Accurate: a yellow and black staircase with handrail, four wheels and landing plates.
guide.board_reading: Panel 1: the ghosted airliner with the stairs highlighted at the forward door. Panel 2: source step 1, the wheel-pin plates, slopes and antenna on the base. Panel 3: source step 2, the staircase part and hinge. Panel 4: the stud map, everything up.
guide.limits: Landing height against the door sill and rolling clearance were not checked.
